strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous benchmark: Evaluates 7 prominent EEG foundation models (BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, EEGPT, CBraMod, CSBrain, REVE) and 2 general time-series models (Mantis, Moment) across 14 public datasets spanning 10 diverse EEG paradigms under standardized preprocessing and evaluation protocols.

Deep diagnostic and mechanistic analysis: Goes well beyond raw accuracy metrics by analyzing gradient dynamics, subspace affinities, gradient conflicts (using CountSketch projection), layer-wise gradient energy, CKA, and RSA, explaining *why* certain architectures and adaptation schemes succeed or fail.

Valuable empirical findings for the community: Provides actionable insights, notably demonstrating that (1) masked reconstruction objectives suffer from substantial gradient misalignment with downstream semantic classification, (2) compact architectures with domain-specific inductive biases (e.g., EEGPT, CBraMod) outperform models scaled on orders-of-magnitude more data (e.g., REVE), and (3) multi-task fine-tuning functions as an effective regularizer against overfitting in data-scarce EEG tasks.

Systematic adaptation and head exploration: Thoroughly assesses three fine-tuning regimes (frozen backbone, LoRA, full-parameter) and multiple decoder architectures across single-task and multi-task setups, isolating the source of performance gains.

Extensive supplementary material and statistical validation: Includes complete numerical tables (with standard deviations over five seeds) across all 14 datasets and extensive qualitative saliency/t-SNE visualizations.
weaknesses: The code link in the abstract is incomplete ('Code is available at' followed by blank space), which should be rectified to ensure full reproducibility and release of the evaluation suite.

The main text relies almost exclusively on dense radar charts (Figures 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) that are visually cluttered and difficult to read without zooming in; presenting aggregate numerical summary tables in the main text would substantially enhance readability.

The benchmark is currently restricted to discrete classification tasks, leaving continuous regression and decoding paradigms (e.g., continuous speech envelope tracking, continuous trajectory decoding in BCI) unexplored.

Differences in native electrode layouts across foundation models necessitate model-specific input adapters (e.g., dynamic routing convolutions for BENDR/BIOT, channel dropping for EEGPT), which introduces slight architectural discrepancies into the downstream comparison.

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark coverage: The paper systematically evaluates seven prominent EEG foundation models (BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, EEGPT, CBraMod, CSBrain, REVE) alongside two general time-series foundation models (Mantis, Moment) across 14 diverse datasets spanning 10 canonical EEG paradigms.

Insightful diagnostic and mechanistic analyses: Instead of merely providing benchmark leaderboards, the authors conduct in-depth diagnostic investigations—using gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity, CKA, RSA, and PCGrad-style gradient conflict analysis—uncovering that gradient conflicts between self-supervised reconstruction objectives and downstream classification tasks impede effective transfer.

Rigorous exploration of adaptation dimensions: The study thoroughly ablates adaptation methods (frozen backbone, parameter-efficient LoRA, full fine-tuning, and training from scratch), decoder head configurations (average pooling, attention pooling, dimension compression MLP), and task formats (single-task vs. multi-task fine-tuning).

Valuable practical takeaways for the domain: The paper challenges conventional scaling assumptions in EEG by demonstrating that compact architectures with domain-specific inductive biases (e.g., EEGPT, CBraMod) outperform significantly larger models (e.g., REVE) trained on much larger corpora, while also highlighting the regularizing benefits of multi-task fine-tuning in data-scarce regimes.
weaknesses: Omission of the promised code repository link: The abstract concludes abruptly with 'Code is available at ' followed by a blank space, and no repository URL or anonymized link is provided in the manuscript. For a submission whose primary contribution is a standardized open-source evaluation suite, the absence of code verification hinders reproducibility.

Over-reliance on dense, hard-to-read radar charts in the main text: The main body relies almost exclusively on small radar plots (Figures 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) with heavily overlapping contours and small font sizes, making precise quantitative comparisons difficult without zooming into the PDF. Including concise numerical summary tables in the main text (which are currently relegated entirely to the appendix) would significantly improve clarity.

Potential confounding from channel adaptation strategies: The 14 evaluated datasets have vastly different channel counts and layouts (ranging from 4 channels in HMC to 64 channels in PhysioMI). Different models utilize distinct mechanisms to handle channel mismatch (e.g., dynamic-routing conv layers for BIOT/BENDR, channel dropping for EEGPT, 1D flattening for LaBraM/CBraMod). The paper does not thoroughly isolate whether downstream performance gaps stem from the pre-trained backbone representations or from these disparate input adaptation layers.

Under-specified multi-task training dynamics: The datasets exhibit severe scale imbalances (e.g., TUSL has ~210 training trials, whereas TUAB has ~247,728 trials). While the authors mention resampling, critical implementation details—such as exact task sampling ratios, per-task batch allocation, and whether smaller tasks experienced gradient starvation or dominance—are insufficiently detailed in the main paper.

strengths: Comprehensive and timely benchmark: Standardizes the evaluation of 7 prominent EEG foundation models and 2 general time-series foundation models across 14 public datasets spanning 10 distinct EEG/BCI paradigms.

Systematic and controlled experimental design: Evaluates models across three fine-tuning regimes (full-parameter, LoRA, linear probe/frozen), two task setups (single-task vs. multi-task joint fine-tuning), and three classification head architectures under identical preprocessing and evaluation partitions.

Insightful mechanistic and diagnostic analyses: Goes far beyond simple leaderboards by investigating optimization dynamics through gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity, layer-wise CKA/RSA alignment, and pre-training vs. downstream gradient conflict analysis.

Important empirical takeaways for the community: Provides concrete evidence challenging naive scaling laws in EEG (compact models with domain inductive biases outperform 14x larger models trained on massive corpora), uncovering significant gradient conflicts between masked reconstruction pre-training and downstream classification, and demonstrating the regularizing effect of multi-task fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Readability of radar charts: Key comparisons across tasks and models in Figures 5, 6, 9, 10, and 11 rely heavily on multi-axis radar charts with overlapping polygons and very small text, which makes fine-grained visual comparison difficult without zooming in heavily; standard grouped bar charts or summary tables in the main text would communicate the results more clearly.

Dimensionality reduction in gradient analysis: In Section 4.3, gradients are projected down to d = 6 dimensions via CountSketch before computing cosine similarities and sign disagreement. A dimension of 6 is extremely low for parameter spaces with millions of weights, raising questions about whether projection noise or hash collisions could artificially skew gradient conflict frequencies.

Analysis across diverse pre-training objectives: The gradient conflict discussion focuses primarily on masked signal reconstruction (MSE) versus classification cross-entropy, but the benchmarked models employ diverse objectives (e.g., contrastive learning in BENDR, token prediction via VQ-VAE in LaBraM). A more granular breakdown comparing contrastive vs. generative/reconstructive objective alignment would clarify whether these conflicts are universal or specific to MSE reconstruction.

Montage adapter disparity: Because different models require different channel montages, varying custom adapters had to be introduced (e.g., dynamic-routing convolutions for BENDR/BIOT, channel dropping for EEGPT, 1D flattening for CBraMod). It remains slightly ambiguous whether differences in adapter design could confound performance comparisons across models.

strengths: Comprehensive and timely benchmark addressing a major reproducibility and standardization gap in the rapidly growing field of EEG foundation models (EEG-FMs).
Extensive experimental scope covering 7 EEG-FMs and 2 general time-series foundation models evaluated across 14 diverse datasets and 10 canonical EEG paradigms.

Rigorous exploration of multiple operational axes: fine-tuning strategies (frozen, LoRA, full-parameter), task organizations (single-task vs. multi-task joint fine-tuning), and classification head architectures.

In-depth diagnostic analysis extending well beyond standard accuracy metrics, incorporating gradient alignment, subspace affinity, conflict frequency, layer-wise CKA/RSA, and neurophysiologically grounded attribution maps.
Principled and transparent handling of pre-training/downstream dataset leakage and overlap-sensitive cases (e.g., isolating SEED and PhysioMI when reporting aggregate rankings).
weaknesses: The code repository URL in the abstract and main text is left blank / truncated ('Code is available at '), which limits immediate verifiability prior to public release.

Main-text presentation relies heavily on dense radar plots (Figures 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) that compress quantitative distinctions across 14 tasks; presenting key summary tables or mean/median aggregate metrics directly in the main body would improve readability.

While the paper thoroughly diagnoses gradient conflicts between pre-training reconstruction and downstream classification, this phenomenon is widely documented in masked signal/image modeling (e.g., MAE in computer vision); the discussion would benefit from a deeper theoretical connection to EEG-specific constraints such as montage mismatch, low SNR, and inter-subject non-stationarity.

Multi-task fine-tuning is implemented with a uniform joint loss and simple resampling; exploring or discussing established multi-task conflict-mitigation algorithms (e.g., PCGrad, GradNorm, or MGDA) would make the multi-task analysis more definitive.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental scope: The benchmark spans 14 public EEG datasets covering 10 distinct paradigms, evaluating seven recent EEG foundation models (BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, EEGPT, CBraMod, CSBrain, REVE) alongside two general time-series foundation models (Mantis, Moment).

Multi-dimensional evaluation protocol: Rather than only testing standard fine-tuning, the authors systematically explore frozen-backbone probing, full-parameter fine-tuning, parameter-efficient tuning (LoRA), training from scratch, single-task vs. multi-task setups, and three different decoder head designs.

Insightful diagnostic and mechanistic analyses: Beyond reporting downstream task metrics, the paper investigates internal optimization dynamics using gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity, gradient conflict frequencies, layer-wise CKA, and RSA. The finding that masked reconstruction objectives produce gradients that actively conflict with semantic classification objectives provides a compelling explanation for why data scaling has yielded diminishing returns in EEG-FMs.

Methodological rigor and fairness: The benchmark properly accounts for class imbalance by utilizing Balanced Accuracy, Weighted F1, AUROC/AUC-PR, and Cohen's Kappa. Crucially, the authors identify pre-training data overlaps (e.g., SEED and PhysioMI in LaBraM/EEGPT) and explicitly exclude overlapping pairs from aggregated scaling comparisons to avoid misleading conclusions.

Strong practical takeaways: The empirical findings offer actionable guidelines for the community—demonstrating that multi-task learning acts as an effective regularizer on low-sample regimes, that frozen representations exhibit large generalization gaps, and that compact, neuro-informed models often rival or surpass scaled-up models.
weaknesses: Visual presentation and readability: Several central figures (Figures 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, and 10 in the main paper) are excessively compressed. The radar plots and 6x6 gradient correlation heatmaps have micro-typography that is virtually unreadable without extreme zooming.

Suboptimal multi-task training baseline: In the multi-task setup, all tasks are jointly optimized using a single shared optimizer and uniform learning schedule. Given the known heterogeneity of EEG montages, sampling rates, and SNR across paradigms, this naive joint training likely exacerbates gradient conflicts and negative transfer, which might be mitigated by existing multi-task optimization techniques (e.g., PCGrad, CAGrad, or loss re-weighting).

Limited exploration of probing capacity: The frozen-backbone analysis primarily evaluates simple pooling with linear/shallow MLP heads. Exploring non-linear MLPs, attentive probes, or k-NN evaluations would clarify whether the observed generalization gap in frozen backbones is purely representational or partially due to linear probe underfitting.

Scope of downstream tasks: While 14 classification datasets across 10 paradigms are included, the benchmark remains entirely classification-oriented and does not cover regression tasks (e.g., continuous cognitive load or reaction time estimation), artifact removal/denoising, or cross-modality retrieval.

strengths: Comprehensive and standardized scope: The benchmark spans 14 public datasets across 10 canonical EEG paradigms (motor imagery, emotion recognition, sleep staging, seizure detection, cognitive workload, Alzheimer's disease, etc.), addressing severe fragmentation and lack of standardized evaluation protocols in the EEG foundation model literature.

Extensive model and setup coverage: Evaluates seven representative EEG foundation models (BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, EEGPT, CBraMod, CSBrain, REVE) alongside two competitive general time-series models across multiple adaptation settings (frozen backbone, LoRA, full-parameter fine-tuning, training from scratch) and decoding head architectures.

Insightful mechanistic and diagnostic analyses: Beyond reporting downstream accuracy tables, the paper investigates optimization dynamics and representation geometry using gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity, Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), and gradient conflict metrics.

Significant empirical findings: The analysis reveals that (1) pre-training reconstruction objectives frequently experience severe gradient conflict with downstream classification objectives, explaining why raw scaling of reconstruction pre-training often yields diminishing downstream returns; (2) frozen representations exhibit a massive generalization gap; and (3) multi-task fine-tuning provides effective regularization for data-scarce paradigms despite potential negative transfer in specialized tasks.

Methodological rigor on overlap sensitivity: The authors explicitly identify and isolate overlapping datasets between pre-training corpora and downstream benchmarks (e.g., SEED, PhysioMI for LaBraM and EEGPT), excluding them from overall performance aggregation to prevent inflated claims.
weaknesses: Scope limited to classification paradigms: All 14 evaluated downstream tasks are discrete classification problems. Downstream tasks involving continuous decoding (e.g., motor kinematics/trajectory regression), signal reconstruction/denoising, or forecasting are not explored.

Confounding factors from model-specific input adapters: Because existing EEG-FMs possess varying native sampling rates, montage assumptions, and channel requirements, the evaluation necessitates custom wrappers (e.g., 1D channel flattening, dynamic-routing Conv1d, or dropping unsupported channels). Consequently, comparisons reflect the combined effect of the pre-trained weights and the adaptation layer rather than the backbone alone.

Details on multi-task optimization balancing: Given the massive scale disparity across datasets (e.g., TUAB with >240,000 samples vs. Workload with ~1,500 samples), the exact sampling strategy and loss weighting across tasks in the multi-task setup could exert a major influence on gradient conflict dynamics; further details and sensitivity analyses regarding task-weighting schedules would strengthen the study.
